vsm1.2:1.1:
Now, while a meditator is engaged in the pursuit of virtue, he should set about undertaking
the ascetic practices in order to perfect those special qualities of fewness of wishes, contentment,
etc., by which the virtue of the kind already described, is cleansed.
vsm1.2:1.2:
For when his virtue is thus washed clean of stains by the waters of such special qualities as fewness of wishes,
contentment, effacement, seclusion, dispersal, energy, and modest needs, it will become quite purified;
vsm1.2:1.3: and his vows will succeed as well.
vsm1.2:1.4:
And so, when his whole behaviour has been purified by the special quality of blameless
virtue and vows and he has become established in the first three of the ancient Noble Ones’ heritages,
he may become worthy to attain to the fourth called “delight in development” (A II 27).
vsm1.2:1.5: We shall therefore begin the explanation of the ascetic practices.
vsm1.2:2.1:
Thirteen kinds of ascetic practices have been allowed by the Blessed One to clansmen who have given up
the things of the flesh and, regardless of body and life, are desirous of undertaking a practice in conformity with their aim.
vsm1.2:2.2:
They are: i. the refuse-rag-wearer’s practice, ii. the triple-robe-wearer’s practice, iii.
the alms-food-eater’s practice, iv. the house-to-house-seeker’s practice, v. the one-sessioner’s practice,
vsm1.2:2.3:
vi. the bowl-food-eater’s practice, vii. the later-food-refuser’s practice, viii.
the forest-dweller’s practice, ix. the tree-root-dweller’s practice,
vsm1.2:2.4:
x. the open-air-dweller’s practice, xi. the charnel-ground-dweller’s practice, xii.
the any-bed-user’s practice, xiii. the sitter’s practice.
vsm1.2:3.1:
Herein:
(1) As to meaning, (2) characteristic, et cetera,
(3) The undertaking and directions,
And then the grade, and breach as well,
And benefits of each besides,
(4) As to the profitable triad,
(5) “Ascetic” and so on distinguished,
(6) And as to groups, and also (7) singly,
The exposition should be known.
vsm1.2:4.1:
Herein, as to meaning, in the first place. i. It is “refuse” (paṃsukūla) since,
owing to its being found on refuse in any such place as a street, a charnel ground, or a midden, it belongs,
as it were, to the refuse in the sense of being dumped in anyone of these places.
vsm1.2:4.2:
Or alternatively: like refuse it gets to a vile state (PAṂSU viya KUcchitabhāvaṃ ULAti),
thus it is “refuse” (paṃsukūla); it goes to a vile state, is what is meant.
vsm1.2:4.3:
The wearing of a refuse-rag, which has acquired its derivative name in this way, is “refuse-rag-wearing”
(paṃsukūla). That is his habit, thus he is a “refuse-rag-wear-er” (paṃsukūlika). The practice
(aṅga) of the refuse-rag-wear-er is the “refuse-rag-wear-er’s practice” (paṃsukūlikaṅga).
vsm1.2:4.4:
It is the action that is called the “practice.” Therefore it should be understood
as a term for that by undertaking which one becomes a refuse-rag-wear-er.
vsm1.2:4.5:
ii. In the same way, he has the habit of wearing the triple robe (ti-cīvara)—in other words, the cloak of patches,
the upper garment, and the inner clothing— thus he is a “triple-robe-wear-er” (tecīvarika).
vsm1.2:4.6: His practice is called the “triple-robe-wearer’s practice.”
vsm1.2:5.1: iii. The dropping (pāta) of the lumps (piṇḍa) of material sustenance (āmisa) called alms (bhikkhā) is “alms food” (piṇḍapāta);
vsm1.2:5.2: the falling (nipatana) into the bowl of lumps (piṇḍa) given by others, is what is meant.
vsm1.2:5.3:
He gleans that alms food (that falling of lumps), he seeks it by approaching such and such
a family, thus he is called an “alms-food eat-er” (piṇḍapātika).
vsm1.2:5.4:
Or his vow is to gather (patituṃ) the lump (piṇḍa), thus he is a “lump-gatherer” (piṇḍapātin). To “gather”
is to wander for. A “lump-gatherer” (piṇḍapātin) is the same as an “alms-food-eater” (piṇḍapātika).
The practice of the alms-food-eater is the “alms-food-eater’s practice.”
vsm1.2:6.1: iv. It is a hiatus (avakhaṇḍana) that is called a “gap” (dāna).
vsm1.2:6.2: It is removed (apeta) from a gap, thus it is called “gapless” (apadāna); the meaning is, it is without hiatus.
vsm1.2:6.3:
It is together with (saha) what is gapless (apadāna), thus it is “with the gapless” (sapadāna);
devoid of hiatus—from house to house—is what is meant.
vsm1.2:6.4:
His habit is to wander on what-is-with-the-gapless, thus he is a “gapless wanderer” (sapadāna-cārin). A gapless wanderer
is the same as a “house-to-house-seeker” (sapadāna-cārika). His practice is the “house-to-house-seeker’s practice.”
vsm1.2:7.1: v. Eating in one session is “one-session.”
vsm1.2:7.2: He has that habit, thus he is a “one-sessioner.” His practice is the “one-sessioner’s practice.”
vsm1.2:7.3: vi. Alms (piṇḍa) in one bowl (patta) only because of refusing a second vessel, is “bowl-alms” (patta-piṇḍa).
vsm1.2:7.4:
Now, making “bowl alms” (patta-piṇḍa) the name for the taking of alms food in the bowl: bowl-alms-food is his habit,
thus he is a “bowl-food-eater” (pattapiṇḍika). His practice is the “bowl-food-eater’s practice.”
vsm1.2:8.1: vii. “No” (khalu) is a particle in the sense of refusing.
vsm1.2:8.2:
Food (bhatta) obtained later by one who has shown that he is satisfied is called “later-food” (pacchā-bhatta).
The eating of that later food is “later-food-eating.” Making “later-food” (pacchā-bhatta) the name for that later-food-eating:
later-food is his habit, thus he is a “later-food-eat-er” (pacchābhattika).
vsm1.2:8.3:
Not a later-food-eater is a “no-later-food-eat-er” (khalu-pacchābhattika), that is, a “later-food-refuser”.
This is the name for one who as an undertaking refuses extra food.
vsm1.2:8.4:
But it is said in the commentary “Khalu is a certain kind of bird. When it has taken
a fruit into its beak and that drops, it does not eat any more.
vsm1.2:8.5:
This bhikkhu is like that.” Thus he is “a later-food-refuser” (khalu-pacchā-bhattika).
His practice is the “later-food-refuser’s practice.”
vsm1.2:9.1: viii. His habit is dwelling in the forest, thus he is a “forest-dweller.” His practice is the “forest-dweller’s practice.”
vsm1.2:9.2: ix. Dwelling at the root of a tree is “tree-root-dwelling.”
vsm1.2:9.3:
He has that habit, thus he is a “tree-root-dweller.” The practice of the tree-root-dweller is the “tree-root-dweller’s
practice.” x., xi. Likewise with the open-air-dweller and the charnel-ground-dweller.
vsm1.2:10.1: xii. Only what has been distributed (yad eva santhata) is “as distributed” (yathāsanthata).
vsm1.2:10.2:
This is a term for the resting place first allotted thus “This one falls to you.”
He has the habit of dwelling in that as distributed, thus he is an “as-distributed-user” (yathāsanthatika),
that is, an “any-bed-user”. His practice is the “any-bed-user’s practice.”
vsm1.2:10.3:
xiii. He has the habit of keeping to the sitting posture when resting, refusing to lie down,
thus he is a “sitter.” His practice is the “sitter’s practice.”
vsm1.2:11.1:
All these, however, are the practices (aṅga) of a bhikkhu who is ascetic (dhuta) because he has shaken off (dhuta)
defilement by undertaking one or other of them. Or the knowledge that has got the name “ascetic” (dhuta) because it shakes
off (dhunana) defilement is a practice (aṅga) belonging to these, thus they are “ascetic practices” (dhutaṅga).
vsm1.2:11.2:
Or alternatively, they are ascetic (dhuta) because they shake off (niddhunana) opposition, and they are practices (aṅga)
because they are a way (paṭipatti). This, firstly, is how the exposition should be known here as to meaning.
vsm1.2:12.1: All of them have as their characteristic the volition of undertaking.
vsm1.2:12.2:
For this is said in the commentary: “He who does the undertaking is a person.
That whereby he does the undertaking is states of consciousness and consciousness-concomitants.
The volition of the act of undertaking is the ascetic practice. What it rejects is the instance.”
vsm1.2:12.3: All have the function of eliminating cupidity,
vsm1.2:12.4:
and they manifest themselves with the production of non-cupidity. For their proximate cause they have the noble states
consisting of fewness of wishes, and so on. This is how the exposition should be known as to characteristic, etc., here.
vsm1.2:13.1:
As regards the five beginning with the undertaking and directions: during the Blessed One’s lifetime
all ascetic practices should be undertaken in the Blessed One’s presence.
vsm1.2:13.2: After his attainment of Nibbāna this should be done in the presence of a principal disciple.
vsm1.2:13.3:
When he is not available it should be done in the presence of one whose cankers
are destroyed, of a non-returner, of a once-returner, of a stream-enterer,
vsm1.2:13.4:
of one who knows the three Piṭakas, of one who knows two of the Piṭakas, of one who knows
one of the Piṭakas, of one who knows one Collection, of a teacher of the Commentaries.
vsm1.2:13.5: When he is not available it should be done in the presence of an observer of an ascetic practice.
vsm1.2:13.6:
When he is not available, then after one has swept out the shrine terrace they can be undertaken seated in a reverential posture
as though pronouncing them in the Fully Enlightened One’s presence. Also it is permitted to undertake them by oneself.
vsm1.2:13.7:
And here should be told the story of the senior of the two brothers who were elders at Cetiyapabbata
and their fewness of wishes with respect to the ascetic practices (M-a II 140).
vsm1.2:13.8: This, firstly, is what applies to all the practices.
vsm1.2:14.1: Now, we shall proceed to comment on the undertaking, directions, grade, breach and benefits, of each one separately.
vsm1.2:14.2: i. First, the refuse-rag-wearer’s practice is undertaken with one of these two statements: “I refuse robes given by householders”
vsm1.2:15.1:
One who has done this should get a robe of one of the following kinds: one from a charnel ground,
one from a shop, a cloth from a street, a cloth from a midden, one from a childbed, an ablution cloth,
a cloth from a washing place, one worn going to and returning from the charnel ground,
vsm1.2:15.2:
one scorched by fire, one gnawed by cattle, one gnawed by ants, one gnawed by rats,
one cut at the end, one cut at the edge, one carried as a flag,
vsm1.2:15.3:
a robe from a shrine, an ascetic’s robe, one from a consecration, one produced by supernormal power,
one from a highway, one borne by the wind, one presented by deities,
vsm1.2:15.4:
one from the sea. Taking one of these robe cloths, he should tear off and throw away the weak parts, and then wash
the sound parts and make up a robe. He can use it after getting rid of his old robe given by householders.
vsm1.2:16.1: Herein, “one from a charnel ground” is one dropped on a charnel ground.
vsm1.2:16.2: “One from a shop” is one dropped at the door of a shop.
vsm1.2:16.3: “A cloth from a street” is a cloth thrown into a street from inside a window by those who seek merit.
vsm1.2:16.4: “A cloth from a midden” is a cloth thrown onto a place for rubbish.
vsm1.2:16.5: “One from a childbed” is a cloth thrown away after wiping up the stains of childbirth with it.
vsm1.2:16.6:
The mother of Tissa the Minister, it seems, had the stains of childbirth wiped up with a cloth worth a hundred
pieces, and thinking, “The refuse-rag wearers will take it,” she had it thrown onto the Tālaveli Road.
vsm1.2:16.7: Bhikkhus took it for the purpose of mending worn places.
vsm1.2:17.1:
“An ablution cloth” is one that people who are made by devil doctors to bathe themselves,
including their heads, are accustomed to throw away as a “cloth of ill luck.”
vsm1.2:17.2: “A cloth from washing place” is rags thrown away at a washing place where bathing is done.
vsm1.2:17.3: “One worn going to and coming from” is one that people throw away after they have gone to a charnel ground and returned and bathed.
vsm1.2:17.4: “One scorched by fire” is one partly scorched by fire; for people throw that away.
vsm1.2:17.5: “One gnawed by cattle,” etc., are obvious; for people throw away such as these too.
vsm1.2:17.6: “One carried as a flag”: Those who board a ship do so after hoisting a flag.
vsm1.2:17.7: It is allowable to take this when they have gone out of sight.
vsm1.2:17.8: Also it is allowable, when the two armies have gone away, to take a flag that has been hoisted on a battlefield.
vsm1.2:18.1: “A robe from a shrine” is an offering made by draping a termite-mound in cloth.
vsm1.2:18.2: “An ascetic’s robe” is one belonging to a bhikkhu.
vsm1.2:18.3: “One from a consecration” is one thrown away at the king’s consecration place.
vsm1.2:18.4: “One produced by supernormal power” is a “come-bhikkhu” robe.
vsm1.2:18.5: “One from a highway” is one dropped in the middle of a road.
vsm1.2:18.6: But one dropped by the owner’s negligence should be taken only after waiting a while.
vsm1.2:18.7: “One borne by the wind” is one that falls a long way off, having been carried by the wind.
vsm1.2:18.8: It is allowable to take it if the owners are not in sight.
vsm1.2:18.9: “One presented by deities” is one given by deities like that given to the Elder Anuruddha (Dhp-a II 173–74).
vsm1.2:18.10: “One from the sea” is one washed up on dry land by the sea waves.
vsm1.2:19.1: One given thus “We give it to the Order” or got by those who go out for alms-cloth is not a refuse-rag.
vsm1.2:19.2:
And in the case of one presented by a bhikkhu, one given after it
has been got at a presentation of robes by householders at the end of the Rains,
vsm1.2:19.3:
or a “resting-place robe” that is, one automatically supplied by a householder
to the occupant of a certain resting place is not a refuse-rag.
vsm1.2:19.4: It is a refuse-rag only when given after not having been so obtained.
vsm1.2:19.5: And herein, that placed by the donors at a bhikkhu’s feet
vsm1.2:19.6: but given by that bhikkhu to the refuse-rag wearer by placing it in his hand is called pure in one way.
vsm1.2:19.7: That given to a bhikkhu by placing it in his hand but placed by him at the refuse-rag wearer’s feet is also pure in one way.
vsm1.2:19.8: That which is both placed at a bhikkhu’s feet and then given by him in the same way is pure in both ways.
vsm1.2:19.9: One obtained by being placed in the hand and given by being placed in the hand too is not a strict man’s robe.
vsm1.2:19.10:
So a refuse-rag wearer should use the robe after getting to know about the kinds of refuse-rags.
These are the directions for it in this instance.
vsm1.2:20.1: The grades are these. There are three kinds of refuse-rag wearers: the strict, the medium, and the mild.
vsm1.2:20.2: Herein, one who takes it only from a charnel ground is strict.
vsm1.2:20.3: One who takes one left by someone, thinking “One gone forth will take it” is medium.
vsm1.2:20.4: One who takes one given by being placed at his feet by a bhikkhu is mild.
vsm1.2:20.5:
The moment anyone of these of his own choice or inclination agrees to accept a robe
given by a householder, his ascetic practice is broken.
vsm1.2:20.6: This is the breach in this instance.
vsm1.2:21.2: there is no fear of robbers; there is no craving connected with use of robes; it is a requisite suitable for an ascetic;
vsm1.2:21.3: it is a requisite recommended by the Blessed One thus “valueless, easy to get, and blameless” (A II 26); it inspires confidence;
vsm1.2:21.4: it produces the fruits of fewness of wishes, etc.; the right way is cultivated; a good example is set to later generations.
vsm1.2:22.1:
While striving for Death’s army’s rout
The ascetic clad in rag-robe clout
Got from a rubbish heap, shines bright
As mail-clad warrior in the fight.
vsm1.2:22.2:
This robe the world’s great teacher wore,
Leaving rare Kāsi cloth and more;
Of rags from off a rubbish heap
Who would not have a robe to keep?
vsm1.2:22.3:
Minding the words he did profess
When he went into homelessness,
Let him to wear such rags delight
As one in seemly garb bedight.
vsm1.2:22.4:
This, firstly, is the commentary on the undertaking, directions, grades,
breach, and benefits, in the case of the refuse-rag-wearer’s practice.
